Dry thunderstorms produced numerous lightning strikes across the Six Rivers National Forest. Twenty-seven fires developed within the Gasquet Ranger District creating the Smith River Complex. The complex grew in size rapidly in the first couple of weeks of the fire, jumping U.S. highway 199 causing it's closure for 3 weeks and resulting in the evacuation of the town of Gasquet. The fire also destroyed the high tension powerlines powering all of Del Norte County. The county was completely without power through August 25th when generators were installed to power the community. Main transmission lines were not repaired until September 10th when full power was restored. The fire continued to burn through September into October with fewer impacts to the community with a total of 95,000 acres burned plus 2 residences and 3 minor structures destroyed.

A thunderstorm impacted Big Bar and produced a hail event that lasted for 30 minutes. The estimated hail size was as large as a golf ball. The hail covered the ground to a depth of 2 inches with drifts up to 6 inches deep.

There were a few reports of snowfall meeting warning criteria, especially at lower elevations. Chain restrictions were required on some of the main roads and numerous traffic accidents were reported on these roads.
The Crescent City ASOS reported a gust to 58 MPH.  There were numerous power outages and trees blown down.

RAWS on the highest mountain peaks reported gusts up to 75-85 mph.

The Crescent City ASOS reported a gust to 64 mph.  Law enforcement reported a large limb of a Redwood tree fell on a Humboldt State University residence hall.  This caused damage to the third floor of the building.  They also reported numerous trees were blown down.

Law enforcement reported several large Redwood trees blew down and closed Highway 128 (next to the Navarro River).  Two vehicles were trapped in between the trees and one of the vehicles received significant damage.  They also reported numerous power outages and trees blown down.
RAWS on the highest mountain peaks reported gusts up to 70-76 mph.  The public reported a giant Redwood tree blew over in Redway.  Law enforcement reported a power outage.
Law enforcement reported a tree blew down onto Highway 101 south of Leggett.  A vehicle crashed into this tree.  They also reported numerous trees were blown down.

Numerous snowfall reports met warning criteria. Snowfall totals of up to 16 inches were reported. Snow levels were down to 1500 to 2000 feet in general. Precipitation initially started off as rain before snow levels lowered. Chain requirements were up for Hwy's 36, 199, and 299, ranging from R-1 to R-2. Hwy 36 was shut down overnight 12/24 to 12/25 at Dinsmore due to heavy snow bringing a tree down over the highway and dragging the power lines down with it. This resulted in a widespread power outage from Bridgeville to Dinsmore. There were multiple CHP reports of vehicle spinouts  and vehicles in the ditch on Hwy 299 near Berry Summit.

There were a few snowfall reports that met warning criteria. Snowfall amounts up to a foot were found near South Fork Mountain in western Trinity County. Snow levels were down to as low as the valley floor in Trinity County with chain requirements on Hwy's 3, 36, and 299 ranging from R-1 to R-2. At one point during the day of 12/24, due to heavy snowfall and numerous car and semi-truck spinouts, CHP and Caltrans shut down the pass over Oregon Mountain for 30 minutes to an hour to clear the road.

There were a few snowfall reports that met warning criteria. The highest snowfall total was eight inches up on Iron Peak near Laytonville. Snow levels were down to as low as the pass levels on Hwy 101 in Mendocino County. CHP contemplated closing Hwy 101 at Ridgewood Summit briefly during the afternoon of 12/24.
Pea to quarter sized hail stones were reported by the public due to a thunderstorm. Photo included coins to reference the hail stone size.

A frontal passage brought high winds meeting warning criteria to Crescent City and areas around Humboldt Bay with numerous reports of trees down and power outages. Damage was most widespread from the Arcata Bottoms to Blue Lake.

Due to a combination of high astronomical tides and high surf, water and debris washed onto some of the area roads. Known roads impacted were Pebble Beach Drive in Crescent City, Highway 101 south of Crescenty City, and Centerville Beach Road near Ferndale.
A combination of high astronomical tides, high surf, and elevated water levels in the Navarro River led to the flooding and closure of a portion of Hwy 128 in Mendocino County.

Additional gusts over 70 mph were reported by the RAWS on Ship Mountain but the observations were questionable due to a sensor malfunction and thus they were not reported as official peak gusts. A public report including photos through social media indicated flooding was occurring on Fred Haight Drive in Smith River after 10-12 inches of rain fell across the county over the previous three days.

Multiple roads around Humboldt Bay were closed due to flooding beginning December 15th in the morning. Roads gradually reopened through the early afternoon on December 16th as water receded. Roads closed included Hookton, Meridian, Port Kenyon, Coffee Creek, Pine Hill, Jackson Ranch, and Berta. Several other roads were also covered in water but remained open. Many of these roads typically flood during heavy rain events. Thus no damage was reported.

The primary highway along the coast, California Route 1, was closed at the Garcia River due to flooding for nearly 24 hours. The exact time of reopening is not known but it was sometime during the day on the 16th of December.

California Route 175 closed due to flooding of the Russian River. No damage reported.

Many roads flooded in the King Salmon area including Cod, Perch and Halibut. Water 6 to 12 inches deep in place with water up to doorsteps. No damage reported. Tide peaked at 9.56ft MLLW at the North Spit tide gauge in Humboldt Bay.

Large surf impacted the coast in conjunction with a small storm surge. This resulted in damage to coastal bluffs along the Del Norte Coast.

Numerous small streams flooded due to heavy rainfall resulting in culvert and manhole failures in Crescent City and neighboring communities. Additionally, a sinkhole allowed debris to flow into the waste water treatment plant causing damage.

Snow chains were required along Highway 36 during much of the event.
